episodes.title: Why Your Game Screen Splits in Two
episodes.description:
That horizontal split is two rendered frames sharing one display refresh. This short animation shows how a fixed-refresh screen scans an image, how the GPU can replace that image mid-scan and why V-Sync and VRR solve the timing mismatch in different ways.

episodes.title: Why V-Sync Can Make Controls Feel Slower
episodes.description:
V-Sync removes tearing by waiting for a display refresh boundary, but a narrowly missed deadline or deep frame queue can make fresh input wait. This short animation explains why the delay is not one fixed number and how refresh rate changes the size of each timing window.

episodes.title: How VRR Makes a Monitor Wait for the GPU
episodes.description:
Variable refresh rate does not make the GPU faster. It lets a compatible display begin a refresh when a frame is ready. This short animation explains the VRR operating window, why low and high frame rates still matter and which parts of the display path must support it.

episodes.title: Why HDR Games Still Need Tone Mapping
episodes.description:
An HDR scene can contain more luminance than one real display can reproduce. This short animation shows how tone mapping fits highlights, mid-tones and dark detail into the screen's measured brightness range instead of simply clipping everything above its limit.

episodes.title: How Anti-Aliasing Removes Stair-Step Edges
episodes.description:
A diagonal edge has to fit a square pixel grid, which creates visible steps. This short animation compares sub-pixel coverage, screen-space smoothing and temporal history, then explains why MSAA, FXAA and temporal methods trade cost against softness or artefacts.

episodes.title: Why Motion Blur Can Make 30 FPS Look Smoother
episodes.description:
Motion blur cannot create extra frames, yet it can soften the visible jump between two positions. This short animation follows a moving object through a velocity-based blur and shows why the effect does not reduce input latency, repair stutter or handle every scene perfectly.

episodes.title: How Frame Generation Creates In-Between Frames
episodes.description:
Frame generation analyses consecutive rendered frames and motion evidence, then synthesises an intermediate image. This short animation separates displayed smoothness from game simulation, input sampling, frame pacing and the artefacts that can appear when the source evidence is weak.
